stem: A galvanic cell is assembled from Ag+(aq) + e- -> Ag(s) (E deg = +0.80 V) and Ni2+(aq) + 2e- -> Ni(s) (E deg = -0.25 V). Which metal is oxidized, and what is the standard cell potential E deg_cell?
choices: Ni is oxidized; E deg_cell = +1.05 V
Ag is oxidized; E deg_cell = +1.05 V
Ni is oxidized; E deg_cell = +0.55 V
Ni is oxidized; E deg_cell = -1.05 V

choice_diagnosis.misconception: assigns oxidation to the half-cell with the higher reduction potential; reverses which electrode is the anode

explanation: The half-cell with the higher (more positive) reduction potential is reduced at the cathode, so Ag+/Ag (+0.80 V) is the cathode and Ni is oxidized at the anode. E deg_cell = E deg_cathode - E deg_anode = 0.80 - (-0.25) = +1.05 V.
source_location: Ch. 17.2 Galvanic Cells; Ch. 17.3 Standard Reduction Potentials

stem: A spontaneous galvanic cell has a measured standard cell potential E deg_cell = +0.46 V for a reaction transferring n = 2 electrons. Which statement about the standard free-energy change and the equilibrium constant is correct?
choices: Delta-G deg < 0 and K > 1
Delta-G deg > 0 and K < 1
Delta-G deg < 0 and K < 1
Delta-G deg = 0 and K = 1

choice_diagnosis.misconception: thinks a positive E deg_cell gives a positive Delta-G deg; inverts the sign in Delta-G deg = -nFE deg_cell
gets the Delta-G deg sign right but does not connect Delta-G deg < 0 to K > 1
assumes standard conditions mean the cell is at equilibrium

explanation: A positive E deg_cell makes Delta-G deg = -nFE deg_cell negative, so the reaction is spontaneous. Because Delta-G deg = -RT ln K, a negative Delta-G deg requires K > 1.
source_location: Ch. 17.4 The Nernst Equation (Delta-G deg = -nFE deg_cell)

stem: A galvanic cell initially operates at standard conditions. The concentration of the ion being reduced at the cathode is then increased well above 1 M, with everything else held standard. How does the measured cell potential Ecell compare to E deg_cell?
choices: Ecell > E deg_cell
Ecell < E deg_cell
Ecell = E deg_cell
Ecell = 0 V

choice_diagnosis.misconception: reverses the Nernst dependence; thinks more cathode reactant lowers the potential
believes concentration cannot affect cell potential
assumes any concentration change drives the cell to equilibrium

explanation: By the Nernst equation Ecell = E deg_cell - (RT/nF) ln Q. Increasing the concentration of a reactant (the cathode ion being reduced) lowers the reaction quotient Q, and a smaller Q raises Ecell above E deg_cell.
source_location: Ch. 17.4 The Nernst Equation

stem: An ammonia buffer is prepared with [NH3] = 0.20 M and [NH4+] = 0.020 M. For the ammonium ion, pKa = 9.25. What is the pH of the buffer?

choice_diagnosis.misconception: assumes pH always equals pKa, ignoring the base/acid ratio

explanation: Using Henderson-Hasselbalch, pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]) = 9.25 + log(0.20/0.020) = 9.25 + log(10) = 9.25 + 1 = 10.25.
source_location: Ch. 14.6 Buffers (Henderson-Hasselbalch)

stem: A small amount of strong acid (HCl) is added to a carbonate buffer containing comparable amounts of HCO3- and H2CO3. Which best describes the result?
choices: Most of the added H+ is consumed by the conjugate base (HCO3-), so the pH decreases only slightly
The added H+ has no effect, because a buffer holds pH perfectly constant
The pH rises, because adding acid to a buffer increases pH
The pH drops as much as it would if the acid were added to pure water

choice_diagnosis.misconception: believes a buffer fixes pH absolutely rather than resisting change
reverses the direction of pH change when acid is added
thinks the buffer does not neutralize added acid at all

explanation: A buffer resists, but does not prevent, pH change. Added H+ is largely neutralized by the conjugate base HCO3- (converting it to H2CO3), so the pH falls only slightly rather than dropping sharply as it would in unbuffered water.
source_location: Ch. 14.6 Buffers (buffer action)

stem: Acid HA has Ka = 1x10^-3 and acid HB has Ka = 1x10^-7. Which statement is correct?
choices: HB is the weaker acid, so its conjugate base B- is the stronger base
HA is the weaker acid, so its conjugate base A- is the stronger base
HB is the stronger acid because the exponent 7 is larger than 3
The two conjugate bases are equally strong because both acids are weak

choice_diagnosis.misconception: reverses the Ka-to-strength relationship (larger Ka = stronger acid)
misreads 1x10^-7 as larger than 1x10^-3
thinks all weak acids yield equally strong conjugate bases

explanation: A larger Ka means a stronger acid, so HA (Ka = 1x10^-3) is stronger and HB (Ka = 1x10^-7) is weaker. The weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base, so B- is the stronger conjugate base.
source_location: Ch. 14.3 Relative Strengths of Acids and Bases

stem: Dissolving ammonium nitrate in water is endothermic (heat is absorbed) yet increases the disorder of the system. Treating the enthalpy and entropy changes as roughly temperature-independent, when is this dissolution thermodynamically favorable?
choices: Only when the temperature is high enough for the entropy term to outweigh the endothermic enthalpy
Only when the temperature is very low
At every temperature, because disorder increases
At no temperature, because heat is absorbed

choice_diagnosis.misconception: swaps the temperature dependence; treats the endothermic, entropy-increasing case as favored only when cold
assumes an entropy increase alone guarantees favorability at any temperature
assumes an endothermic process can never be favorable

explanation: Free-energy change is enthalpy minus temperature times entropy change. With a positive enthalpy change and a positive entropy change, the process becomes favorable only once the temperature is high enough for the entropy term to exceed the enthalpy cost.
source_location: Ch. 16.4 Free Energy (temperature dependence of spontaneity)

stem: An endergonic reaction (Delta-G = +15 kJ/mol) is coupled to ATP hydrolysis (Delta-G = -30 kJ/mol). What is the overall Delta-G, and is the coupled process spontaneous?
choices: -15 kJ/mol; spontaneous
+45 kJ/mol; nonspontaneous
+15 kJ/mol; nonspontaneous
-45 kJ/mol; spontaneous

choice_diagnosis.misconception: subtracts magnitudes instead of adding signed values
believes coupling cannot change the overall Delta-G

explanation: Free-energy changes of coupled reactions add: +15 + (-30) = -15 kJ/mol. A negative overall Delta-G makes the coupled process spontaneous, which is how cells drive otherwise unfavorable reactions with ATP hydrolysis.
source_location: Ch. 16.4 Free Energy (coupled reactions)

stem: Under a particular set of conditions, the forward direction of a reaction has a free-energy change of -40 kJ/mol. Under those same conditions, what is the free-energy change of the reverse direction, and is the reverse direction favorable?
choices: +40 kJ/mol; not favorable
-40 kJ/mol; favorable
+40 kJ/mol; favorable
0 kJ/mol; the reverse direction is at equilibrium

choice_diagnosis.misconception: thinks the reverse reaction has the same free-energy change as the forward reaction
flips the sign correctly but still calls a positive free-energy change favorable
assumes reversing a reaction means it sits at equilibrium

explanation: Reversing a reaction negates its free-energy change, so the reverse direction is +40 kJ/mol. A positive free-energy change is not favorable, so under these conditions the reverse direction does not proceed spontaneously.
source_location: Ch. 16.4 Free Energy (sign of Delta-G for reverse reactions)

stem: A reaction is first order in reactant A with a half-life of 20 s. If the initial concentration of A is doubled, the half-life becomes:
choices: 20 s (unchanged)
explanation: For a first-order reaction, t(1/2) = 0.693/k is independent of the initial concentration, so doubling [A]0 leaves the half-life at 20 s. Only zero- and second-order half-lives depend on concentration.
source_location: Ch. 12.4 Integrated Rate Laws (half-life)

stem: When the concentration of reactant A is doubled (all else constant), the initial rate quadruples. What is the reaction order with respect to A?
choices: Second order
First order
Zero order
Fourth order

choice_diagnosis.misconception: assumes rate is proportional to concentration (first order)
thinks rate independent of concentration despite the change

explanation: Rate is proportional to [A]^n, so doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 2^n. Since the rate increased 4x = 2^2, n = 2 and the reaction is second order in A.
source_location: Ch. 12.3 Rate Laws (method of initial rates)

stem: Adding a catalyst speeds up a reversible reaction. Which statement correctly describes the effect on the rate constants and the equilibrium position?
choices: It lowers the activation energy, raising the forward and reverse rate constants equally, leaving the equilibrium position unchanged
It raises the forward rate constant only, shifting equilibrium toward products
It increases the equilibrium constant K
It speeds the reaction by raising the activation energy

choice_diagnosis.misconception: thinks a catalyst shifts equilibrium toward products
believes a catalyst changes the value of K
reverses the catalyst's effect on activation energy

explanation: A catalyst provides a lower-activation-energy pathway, increasing both the forward and reverse rate constants by the same factor. It speeds the approach to equilibrium but does not change K or the equilibrium position.
source_location: Ch. 12.7 Catalysis (effect on rate vs equilibrium)

stem: An incompressible fluid flows steadily through a horizontal pipe whose cross-sectional area narrows to one-third of its original value. Compared with the wide section, the fluid speed in the narrow section is:
choices: 3 times greater
1/3 as great
unchanged
9 times greater

choice_diagnosis.misconception: thinks flow speed is unaffected by cross-sectional area

explanation: The continuity equation A1*v1 = A2*v2 requires that reducing the area to one-third triples the speed, because the same volume flow rate must pass through the smaller opening.
source_location: Ch. 12.1 Flow Rate and the Equation of Continuity

stem: In the same horizontal pipe, the fluid moves faster in the narrow section than in the wide section. How does the fluid pressure in the narrow (fast) section compare to that in the wide (slow) section?
choices: Lower, because faster-moving fluid has lower pressure
Higher, because narrowing the pipe squeezes and compresses the fluid
Unchanged, because the pipe is horizontal
Zero, because all the pressure energy becomes kinetic energy

choice_diagnosis.misconception: intuits that pressure rises where a pipe narrows
thinks horizontal flow means pressure cannot vary along the pipe
believes speeding up drops pressure all the way to zero

explanation: For horizontal flow, Bernoulli's equation reduces to P + (1/2)*rho*v^2 = constant, so where the speed v is higher the pressure P is lower. The narrow, faster section therefore has lower pressure than the wide section.
source_location: Ch. 12.2 Bernoulli's Equation

stem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose radius decreases by half. By what factor does the flow speed change in the narrower part?
choices: Increases 4x
Increases 2x
Decreases to 1/2
Unchanged

choice_diagnosis.misconception: scales area with radius linearly instead of with radius squared
thinks flow speed is independent of pipe radius

explanation: Cross-sectional area scales with the square of the radius, so halving the radius reduces the area to one-fourth. By continuity (A*v = constant), the speed must increase fourfold.
source_location: Ch. 12.1 Flow Rate and the Equation of Continuity

stem: Glycolysis generates 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation but consumes 2 ATP in its early (energy-investment) steps. What is the net ATP yield per glucose from glycolysis alone?
choices: 2 ATP
4 ATP
6 ATP
0 ATP

choice_diagnosis.misconception: thinks the ATP investment cancels the entire ATP payoff

explanation: Glycolysis invests 2 ATP in the energy-investment phase and produces 4 ATP in the payoff phase, for a net gain of 4 - 2 = 2 ATP per glucose (along with 2 NADH).
source_location: Ch. 7.2 Glycolysis (energy investment vs payoff)

stem: In the absence of oxygen, cells reduce pyruvate to lactate (or ethanol). Why is this step necessary to keep glycolysis running?
choices: It regenerates NAD+ so the oxidation step of glycolysis can continue
It directly produces most of the cell's ATP from pyruvate
It generates the oxygen needed for the electron transport chain
It converts lactate back into glucose to fuel glycolysis

choice_diagnosis.misconception: thinks fermentation itself is a major ATP-producing step
believes fermentation makes oxygen for the ETC
confuses fermentation with gluconeogenesis

explanation: Glycolysis needs NAD+ for its glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step. Without oxygen, NADH cannot be reoxidized by the electron transport chain, so cells reduce pyruvate to regenerate NAD+ and keep glycolytic ATP production going.
source_location: Ch. 7.2 Glycolysis; Ch. 7.5 Fermentation (NAD+ regeneration)

stem: Phosphofructokinase (PFK) catalyzes a committed step of glycolysis and is inhibited by high levels of ATP. What is the physiological consequence when cellular ATP is abundant?
choices: Glycolysis slows, conserving glucose when energy is already plentiful
Glycolysis speeds up to produce even more ATP
PFK is unaffected because ATP is a substrate, not a regulator
Glucose is converted directly into ATP, bypassing glycolysis

choice_diagnosis.misconception: reverses feedback logic; expects abundant ATP to accelerate its own production
does not recognize ATP as an allosteric regulator of PFK
thinks ATP can be made from glucose without the glycolytic pathway

explanation: PFK controls the rate-limiting, committed step of glycolysis. Abundant ATP allosterically inhibits PFK (feedback inhibition), slowing glycolysis when the cell's energy charge is already high.
source_location: Ch. 7.2 Glycolysis (regulation of PFK)

stem: One turn of the citric acid cycle produces 3 NADH and 1 FADH2. If each NADH yields about 2.5 ATP and each FADH2 about 1.5 ATP through oxidative phosphorylation, how much ATP comes from these carriers per turn?
choices: About 9 ATP
About 4 ATP
About 10 ATP
About 1 ATP

choice_diagnosis.misconception: counts the number of electron carriers rather than the ATP they yield
counts only the substrate-level GTP and ignores the carriers

explanation: 3 NADH x 2.5 + 1 FADH2 x 1.5 = 7.5 + 1.5 = 9 ATP from oxidative phosphorylation per turn (plus 1 GTP from substrate-level phosphorylation).
source_location: Ch. 7.3 Oxidation of Pyruvate and the Citric Acid Cycle; Ch. 7.4 OXPHOS

stem: The citric acid cycle uses no O2 in any of its own reactions, yet it halts quickly when O2 is absent. Why?
choices: Without the O2-dependent electron transport chain, NAD+ and FAD are not regenerated, so the cycle runs out of oxidized carriers
The cycle enzymes require O2 directly as a substrate
Pyruvate cannot be produced in the absence of O2
CO2 cannot be released from the cycle without O2

choice_diagnosis.misconception: thinks citric acid cycle enzymes consume O2 directly
believes glycolysis (pyruvate production) requires O2
thinks CO2 release from the cycle depends on O2

explanation: The cycle depends on a supply of NAD+ and FAD. These are regenerated only when NADH/FADH2 hand electrons to the electron transport chain, whose terminal acceptor is O2. Without O2 the oxidized carriers run out and the cycle stalls, even though no cycle enzyme uses O2 directly.
source_location: Ch. 7.3 Citric Acid Cycle; Ch. 7.4 Oxidative Phosphorylation

stem: Per turn of the citric acid cycle, two carbons enter as the acetyl group of acetyl-CoA. How many carbons leave as CO2, and what does this imply?
choices: Two carbons leave as CO2, matching the two that entered, so oxaloacetate is regenerated and the cycle can repeat
No carbons leave; they are all stored in cycle intermediates
Four carbons leave as CO2, depleting the cycle intermediates
Two enter but only one leaves, so oxaloacetate steadily accumulates

choice_diagnosis.misconception: does not track that carbons exit the cycle as CO2
miscounts CO2 released per turn
thinks carbon input and output are unbalanced, so an intermediate accumulates

explanation: Each turn releases two CO2 (at the isocitrate -> alpha-ketoglutarate and alpha-ketoglutarate -> succinyl-CoA steps), balancing the two carbons of the acetyl group that entered. This regenerates oxaloacetate so the cycle can continue.
source_location: Ch. 7.3 Oxidation of Pyruvate and the Citric Acid Cycle (carbon accounting)

stem: A reversible inhibitor binds an enzyme at a site other than the active site, and its effect cannot be overcome by adding more substrate. How does it affect Vmax and Km?
choices: Lowers Vmax; Km is unchanged
Vmax is unchanged; Km increases
Both Vmax and Km increase
Both Vmax and Km decrease

choice_diagnosis.misconception: describes competitive inhibition (Vmax unchanged, Km up) instead of noncompetitive
does not know noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax
describes uncompetitive inhibition (both lowered) instead

explanation: An inhibitor that binds away from the active site and is not relieved by excess substrate is noncompetitive. It effectively removes functional enzyme, lowering Vmax, while substrate affinity (Km) is unchanged.
source_location: Ch. 6.5 Enzymes (competitive vs noncompetitive inhibition)

stem: An enzyme early in a biosynthetic pathway is inhibited when the pathway's final product accumulates. This regulation is best described as:
choices: Allosteric feedback inhibition that prevents overproduction of the end product
Competitive inhibition by the pathway substrate
Irreversible covalent inactivation of the enzyme
Denaturation of the enzyme by its own product

choice_diagnosis.misconception: confuses the end product acting at a regulatory site with a substrate competing at the active site
mistakes reversible allosteric regulation for irreversible covalent modification
thinks product binding denatures rather than allosterically regulates the enzyme

explanation: The end product binds an allosteric (regulatory) site, changing the enzyme's conformation and reducing its activity. This feedback inhibition lets the cell switch off a pathway once enough product has been made.
source_location: Ch. 6.5 Enzymes (allosteric regulation and feedback inhibition)

stem: A human enzyme is maximally active at 37 C and pH 7. At 60 C its activity falls to nearly zero and does not return when the sample is cooled back to 37 C. The best explanation is:
choices: High temperature denatured the enzyme, disrupting its active-site structure in a way that does not spontaneously reverse
Higher temperature always increases enzyme rate, so the data must be erroneous
The enzyme simply ran out of substrate at 60 C
Cooling should have fully restored activity, so the enzyme was only temporarily slowed

choice_diagnosis.misconception: believes enzyme rate rises with temperature without limit, ignoring denaturation
attributes lost activity to substrate depletion rather than protein structure
assumes denaturation is readily reversible on cooling

explanation: Enzyme rate rises with temperature only until the protein denatures. At 60 C the tertiary structure and active site are disrupted; because such denaturation is generally not reversible, activity does not return on cooling.
source_location: Ch. 6.5 Enzymes (temperature, pH, and denaturation)

stem: A red blood cell is placed in a hypertonic solution. What happens to the cell, and why?
choices: It shrinks (crenates) as water moves out toward the higher external solute concentration
It swells and bursts as water moves into the cell
Nothing happens, because the membrane is impermeable to water
It shrinks because solutes are pumped out of the cell

choice_diagnosis.misconception: reverses the direction of osmosis (treats the solution as hypotonic)
thinks the membrane blocks water movement
attributes volume change to solute movement rather than osmotic water movement

explanation: Water moves by osmosis from lower to higher solute concentration. In a hypertonic solution the outside is more concentrated, so water leaves the cell and it shrinks (crenates).
source_location: Ch. 5.2 Passive Transport (osmosis and tonicity)

stem: A solute is moved across a membrane from a region of low concentration to a region of high concentration. Which statement must be true?
choices: The process requires an energy input, such as ATP or a coupled ion gradient
It occurs by simple diffusion down the solute's gradient
It requires no energy because membranes are freely permeable
It occurs only directly through the lipid bilayer, without proteins

choice_diagnosis.misconception: thinks movement against a gradient can occur by passive diffusion
believes transport never requires energy
ignores that against-gradient transport needs membrane proteins

explanation: Moving a solute against its concentration gradient (low to high) is active transport and requires energy, supplied directly by ATP (primary active transport) or by a previously established ion gradient (secondary active transport).
source_location: Ch. 5.3 Active Transport

stem: Glucose entry into a cell via a carrier protein rises with external glucose but levels off at high concentrations, whereas simple diffusion of a small nonpolar gas does not level off. What accounts for the difference?
choices: Carrier proteins are limited in number and become saturated; simple diffusion has no carriers to saturate
Glucose diffuses faster than gases at high concentration
Simple diffusion also saturates, so the observation must be wrong
Glucose is nonpolar and needs no transporter

choice_diagnosis.misconception: does not connect the plateau to a finite number of carrier proteins
thinks simple diffusion also shows saturation kinetics
misclassifies glucose as able to cross the bilayer without a transporter

explanation: Facilitated diffusion depends on a finite number of carrier proteins; once all carriers are occupied, adding more solute cannot increase the rate (saturation). Simple diffusion has no carriers, so its rate keeps rising with concentration.
source_location: Ch. 5.2 Passive Transport (facilitated diffusion)

stem: DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only in the 5' -> 3' direction. At a replication fork, this constraint means that:
choices: One new strand is made continuously (leading) while the other is made in short Okazaki fragments (lagging)
Both new strands are synthesized continuously in the same direction
Both new strands are made entirely as Okazaki fragments
The lagging strand is synthesized in the 3' -> 5' direction

choice_diagnosis.misconception: ignores the antiparallel templates that force discontinuous synthesis on one strand
over-applies discontinuous synthesis to both strands
thinks polymerase can reverse and synthesize 3' -> 5'

explanation: Because the two template strands are antiparallel and polymerase works only 5' -> 3', the strand templated toward the advancing fork is made continuously (leading), while the other is made discontinuously as Okazaki fragments (lagging).
source_location: Ch. 14.4 DNA Replication in Prokaryotes (leading vs lagging strand)

stem: DNA labeled entirely with heavy nitrogen (15N) is allowed to replicate once in a light-nitrogen (14N) medium. What does each daughter duplex contain, and what does this demonstrate?
choices: Each duplex has one heavy (old) and one light (new) strand, demonstrating semiconservative replication
One duplex is fully heavy and one fully light, demonstrating conservative replication
Both strands of each duplex are new, demonstrating dispersive replication
All strands stay heavy, because parental DNA strands are not reused

choice_diagnosis.misconception: predicts the conservative model's fully-heavy/fully-light result
predicts the dispersive model's all-new result
does not recognize that parental strands serve as templates

explanation: Replication is semiconservative: each parental strand templates a new one, so after a single round in 14N every duplex has one original (15N) and one new (14N) strand -- the classic Meselson-Stahl result.
source_location: Ch. 14.3 Basics of DNA Replication (semiconservative model)

stem: DNA polymerase has 3' -> 5' exonuclease (proofreading) activity. A mutation that abolishes this proofreading activity would most likely:
choices: Increase the mutation rate, because misincorporated bases are no longer removed
Halt DNA replication entirely
Have no effect, because base pairing is always perfectly accurate
Decrease the mutation rate

choice_diagnosis.misconception: thinks proofreading is required for the polymerization reaction itself
assumes replication is error-free even without proofreading
reverses the effect: expects fewer mutations without proofreading

explanation: Proofreading exonuclease removes mismatched nucleotides immediately after they are added. Losing this activity leaves errors uncorrected, raising the mutation rate, although polymerization (replication) can still proceed.
source_location: Ch. 14.4 DNA Replication (proofreading by DNA polymerase)

stem: Two organisms heterozygous for a single gene (Aa x Aa) are crossed. What fraction of the offspring is expected to show the recessive phenotype?

choice_diagnosis.misconception: reports the heterozygote genotype fraction instead of the recessive phenotype fraction
reports the dominant phenotype fraction (3/4) by mistake
thinks the recessive phenotype cannot appear from two hybrids

explanation: An Aa x Aa cross gives genotypes in a 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa ratio. Only aa (1/4) shows the recessive phenotype; the other 3/4 show the dominant phenotype.
source_location: Ch. 12.2 Characteristics and Traits (monohybrid cross)

stem: An organism displays the dominant phenotype, but whether it is AA or Aa is unknown. Crossing it with which partner best reveals its genotype?
choices: A homozygous recessive (aa) individual
A homozygous dominant (AA) individual
Another individual with the same dominant phenotype
Only a heterozygote can be used

choice_diagnosis.misconception: chooses a partner whose dominant alleles would mask the unknown recessive allele
does not realize matching dominant phenotypes hide the genotype
wrongly believes only a heterozygote partner works

explanation: A test cross with a homozygous recessive (aa) partner reveals hidden alleles: any recessive offspring means the unknown parent is Aa, whereas all-dominant offspring indicate AA. Crossing with AA would mask the difference.
source_location: Ch. 12.2 Characteristics and Traits (test cross)

stem: In snapdragons, red (CR CR) crossed with white (CW CW) yields all pink (CR CW) F1 plants. If two pink F1 plants are crossed, what phenotype ratio is expected in the F2 generation?
choices: 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white
3 red : 1 white
All pink
1 red : 1 white

choice_diagnosis.misconception: applies complete-dominance 3:1 ratios to an incomplete-dominance cross
treats blending as permanent, expecting only the intermediate phenotype
omits the heterozygous (pink) class from the ratio

explanation: With incomplete dominance the heterozygote (pink) is a distinct phenotype, so the phenotype ratio matches the genotype ratio: CR CR (red) : CR CW (pink) : CW CW (white) = 1 : 2 : 1.
source_location: Ch. 12.3 Laws of Inheritance (incomplete dominance)

stem: A student studies in a silent library but takes the exam in a noisy hall and struggles to recall material she clearly learned. This is best explained by:
choices: Context-dependent memory -- retrieval is aided when the recall environment matches the encoding environment
Encoding failure -- the material was never stored in the first place
Proactive interference from earlier learning
Decay of the memory trace over a few minutes

choice_diagnosis.misconception: attributes the failure to encoding even though the material was learned
misapplies proactive interference to an environment-mismatch case
invokes rapid decay rather than a retrieval-cue mismatch

explanation: Context-dependent memory holds that retrieval improves when the recall context matches the encoding context. The mismatch between the quiet study setting and the noisy exam hall weakens retrieval cues, hindering recall of well-learned material.
source_location: Ch. 8.2 Parts of the Brain Involved with Memory; Ch. 8.3 Recall/Retrieval

stem: One student prepares by repeating definitions verbatim; another links each concept to personal examples. Why does the second student typically remember more?
choices: Elaborative (deep, semantic) rehearsal creates more retrieval routes than rote maintenance rehearsal
Maintenance rehearsal transfers information to long-term memory more reliably than elaboration
Repetition is the only route to long-term storage
Personal examples overload working memory and should reduce recall

choice_diagnosis.misconception: reverses the depth-of-processing effect, favoring rote repetition
believes rote repetition is the sole path to long-term memory
thinks elaboration harms memory by overloading working memory

explanation: Deep, elaborative processing that ties new material to existing knowledge creates stronger, more richly cued long-term memories than shallow maintenance rehearsal (simple repetition), consistent with the levels-of-processing framework.
source_location: Ch. 8.1 How Memory Functions (encoding; levels of processing)

stem: A person recalls the letter string 'FBICIAIRS' far more easily after being told to read it as FBI-CIA-IRS. This improvement is due to:
choices: Chunking -- grouping items into meaningful units expands effective short-term memory capacity
An increase in the raw capacity of sensory memory
The elimination of rehearsal and decay
Transfer of the letters into procedural memory

choice_diagnosis.misconception: attributes the gain to sensory memory rather than chunking of STM
thinks chunking removes decay rather than reorganizing units
misclassifies the recall as procedural (skill) memory

explanation: Short-term memory holds a limited number of units (about 7 +/- 2). Chunking reorganizes individual letters into a few meaningful groups, so more information fits within the same capacity, improving recall.
source_location: Ch. 8.1 How Memory Functions (short-term memory capacity; chunking)

stem: A dog begins to salivate at the sound of a can opener because that sound has repeatedly preceded feeding. This is an example of:
choices: Classical conditioning -- a previously neutral stimulus comes to elicit a reflexive response
Operant conditioning through positive reinforcement
Negative punishment
Observational learning

choice_diagnosis.misconception: classifies a reflexive (involuntary) response as operant conditioning of a voluntary behavior
misapplies punishment to a stimulus-elicited reflex
mistakes stimulus pairing for learning by watching others

explanation: Salivation is an involuntary reflex, and the originally neutral can-opener sound comes to elicit it after being paired with food. That neutral-stimulus-to-reflex pairing defines classical conditioning, not operant conditioning (which involves voluntary behavior and its consequences).
source_location: Ch. 6.2 Classical Conditioning

stem: A teacher cancels the class's weekend homework whenever students behave well, and good behavior then increases. This consequence is best classified as:
choices: Negative reinforcement -- removing an aversive stimulus to increase a behavior
Positive reinforcement
Negative punishment
Positive punishment

choice_diagnosis.misconception: labels any desirable outcome 'positive reinforcement,' ignoring that something was removed
confuses reinforcement (behavior increases) with punishment
confuses reinforcement with punishment and misreads the direction

explanation: Because the target behavior increases, this is reinforcement, not punishment. Since an aversive stimulus (homework) is removed, it is negative reinforcement -- 'negative' means removal, not 'bad.'
source_location: Ch. 6.3 Operant Conditioning (reinforcement vs punishment)

stem: A gambler keeps playing a slot machine that pays out after an unpredictable number of plays. Which reinforcement schedule best explains this persistent, hard-to-extinguish behavior?
choices: Variable-ratio schedule
Fixed-interval schedule
Continuous reinforcement
Negative punishment

choice_diagnosis.misconception: confuses an unpredictable response-based payout with a time-based schedule
thinks every play is rewarded (continuous reinforcement)
misclassifies a reinforcing outcome as punishment

explanation: Slot machines reward after an unpredictable number of responses -- a variable-ratio schedule. Such schedules produce high, steady response rates that are especially resistant to extinction, which is why gambling can be so persistent.
source_location: Ch. 6.3 Operant Conditioning (schedules of reinforcement)

stem: Watching a stranger trip, an observer thinks 'how clumsy,' but when she trips herself she blames the uneven pavement. This pattern reflects:
choices: The fundamental attribution error (actor-observer bias) -- overweighting disposition for others and situation for oneself
The self-serving bias applied to another person
Groupthink
The just-world hypothesis

choice_diagnosis.misconception: misapplies the self-serving bias to explanations of others' behavior
invokes a group decision-making bias for an individual attribution
substitutes the just-world hypothesis for an attribution bias

explanation: Attributing others' behavior to their character while attributing one's own behavior to circumstances is the actor-observer form of the fundamental attribution error -- a systematic bias toward dispositional explanations for other people.
source_location: Ch. 12.1 What Is Social Psychology? (attribution; fundamental attribution error)

stem: An employee reluctantly works late after a direct order from a supervisor. This behavior change is best classified as:
choices: Obedience -- change in response to a direct command from an authority figure
Conformity to peer-group norms
Compliance with a persuasive request from an equal
Internalization of a personal value

choice_diagnosis.misconception: confuses authority-driven obedience with matching peer norms (conformity)
labels an authority's command as a peer request (compliance)
mistakes externally ordered behavior for internalized personal values

explanation: Obedience is behavior change produced by a direct order from a perceived authority. Conformity is matching group norms without an explicit order, and compliance follows a request from a non-authority -- neither fits a supervisor's direct command.
source_location: Ch. 12.3 Conformity, Compliance, and Obedience

stem: After volunteering to do a boring task for very little pay, participants later rate the task as more enjoyable than those who were paid a large sum. The best explanation is:
choices: Cognitive dissonance -- with little external justification, people change their attitude to fit their behavior
Positive reinforcement from receiving the small payment
The mere-exposure effect
Observational learning from other participants

choice_diagnosis.misconception: expects a larger reward to produce greater liking, reversing the dissonance finding
attributes attitude change to mere repeated exposure
attributes the effect to learning by watching others

explanation: Low pay offers little external justification for doing a dull task, creating dissonance that people resolve by deciding they actually enjoyed it. High pay supplies enough justification, so no attitude change is needed -- the classic Festinger-Carlsmith result.
source_location: Ch. 12.2 Self-presentation (attitudes and cognitive dissonance)

stem: A study finds that a neighborhood's ZIP code predicts residents' life expectancy better than their genetic profiles do. Which interpretation is best supported?
choices: Social determinants of health -- income, environment, and access to care -- strongly shape health outcomes
Genetics plays no role in any health outcome
ZIP code itself directly causes disease at the molecular level
Life expectancy is essentially fixed at birth

choice_diagnosis.misconception: overgeneralizes to claim genetics is irrelevant to all health
treats a geographic proxy as a direct molecular cause
assumes life expectancy is immutable, ignoring social conditions

explanation: When place predicts health more strongly than genes, it points to social determinants -- income, environment, food and health-care access -- as major drivers of health disparities, without claiming that genetics is irrelevant.
source_location: Ch. 14.3 Stress and Illness (social determinants of health)

stem: Chronic stress is associated with higher rates of cardiovascular disease. Which mechanism best connects the two?
choices: Prolonged activation of the stress response (e.g., sustained cortisol and elevated blood pressure) damages the cardiovascular system over time
Stress hormones are biologically inert and cannot affect the heart
Stress affects only mood and never physical health
Acute short-term stress and chronic stress harm the body in exactly the same way

choice_diagnosis.misconception: believes stress hormones have no physiological effect on the cardiovascular system
treats stress as purely psychological with no physical consequences
ignores that duration distinguishes adaptive acute stress from harmful chronic stress

explanation: The short-term stress response is adaptive, but chronic activation keeps cortisol and blood pressure elevated, contributing over time to hypertension and cardiovascular disease -- a key physiological link between chronic stress and physical illness.
source_location: Ch. 14.3 Stress and Illness (stress physiology and disease)

stem: Group A shows worse diabetes outcomes than Group B. Before concluding the cause is biological, a researcher should first:
choices: Check whether differences in access to care and socioeconomic status account for the outcome gap
Assume the two groups differ genetically
Conclude that the disparity is fixed and cannot be changed
Treat socioeconomic variables as irrelevant to health outcomes

choice_diagnosis.misconception: jumps to a genetic explanation without ruling out social factors
assumes disparities are immutable rather than socially driven
dismisses socioeconomic status as a determinant of health

explanation: Health disparities frequently reflect unequal social conditions rather than inherent biology. Responsible interpretation first tests whether access to care, income, and other social determinants explain the outcome gap before invoking genetic causes.
source_location: Ch. 14.3 Stress and Illness (interpreting health disparities)
